title: How Many Groups Can the Data Support? — Ferguson’s (1973) Dirichlet Process, Blackwell–MacQueen Pólya Urn Clustering & Escobar–West Nonparametric Mixture Density Estimation of Roeder’s 82 Galaxy Velocities

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: When astronomers measured 82 galaxy velocities, how many hidden galaxy clusters were really there—3, 6, or 9? Instead of forcing one fixed K, Ferguson's Dirichlet Process and Escobar–West mixtures let the posterior average across cluster counts automatically.
teenKit.whyItMatters: From genetics cell types to astronomy clusters, picking K by eye overfits noise or blurs real subgroups; nonparametric Bayes reports uncertainty over K itself.
keyTakeaways: Ferguson (1973) introduced the Dirichlet Process (DP) as a prior over probability distributions, and Blackwell & MacQueen (1973) showed its 'Chinese restaurant / Polya urn' clustering rule.
In a DP Gaussian mixture (Escobar & West 1995), a new observation joins an existing cluster proportional to its size n_j or opens a fresh cluster proportional to concentration alpha.
On Roeder's 82 Corona Borealis galaxy velocities, the posterior distribution over occupied clusters K reveals multimodal substructure without locking into a single K.

vocab.meaning: A stochastic process generating discrete random probability measures, serving as an infinite-capacity prior for mixture models.
Controls the propensity to spawn new clusters in a Polya urn / Chinese restaurant process.
Models whose complexity (such as active mixture components) can grow flexibly with sample size rather than fixing p parameters forever.

quiz.question: In the Blackwell–MacQueen Polya urn scheme with concentration alpha and N existing points, what is the prior probability that point N + 1 starts a brand-new cluster?
quiz.explanation: Existing clusters attract weight proportional to their counts (summing to N), while a new draw from the base measure has weight alpha, giving alpha / (alpha + N).
